text: Belvagene Davis (née Melton; October 13, 1932 – September 24, 2025) was an American television and radio journalist who became the first African-American woman to serve as a television reporter on the U.S. West Coast. Born in Monroe, Louisiana, on October 13, 1932, to John and Florence Melton, she was the oldest of four children; her mother was 14 years old at the time of her birth, and Belva spent her early years living with relatives. At age eight, she and her family moved to a two-bedroom apartment in West Oakland, California, where eleven people lived. Davis graduated from Berkeley High School in 1951, becoming the first in her family to do so. Though accepted into San Francisco State University, she could not afford college and worked as a typist at the Oakland Naval Supply Depot earning $2,000 annually. In 1957, she began writing freelance articles for Jet, a magazine focused on African-American issues, receiving $5 per piece with no byline, and later wrote for publications such as the Sun Reporter and Bay Area Independent, editing the latter from 1961 to 1968. In 1961, she became an on-air interviewer for KSAN, a San Francisco AM radio station targeting Black listeners, and made her television debut in 1963 for KTVU covering an African-American beauty pageant. She worked as a disc jockey for KDIA, a soul-gospel radio station in Oakland, when covering the 1964 Republican National Convention at the Cow Palace, where she and Louis Freeman were chased out by attendees throwing food and shouting racial slurs. In 1966, she joined KNEW as an announcer and became the first female African-American television journalist on the West Coast when hired by KPIX-TV, the CBS affiliate in San Francisco. She later worked for KRON-TV, the local NBC affiliate, becoming an anchorwoman in 1970. Over her career, she covered major events including the Berkeley riots of the Free Speech Movement, the Black Panthers, the Jonestown mass suicide-murder, the Moscone–Milk assassinations, the AIDS and crack epidemics, and the 1998 U.S. embassy bombing in Tanzania. From 1981 to 1999, she co-hosted KRON’s Sunday-morning show "California This Week" with Rollin Post. In the 1990s, she hosted "This Week in Northern California" on PBS member station KQED, retiring in November 2012. Her final broadcast featured a taped interview with Maya Angelou, a personal friend, to emphasize the theme of friendship. Davis was recognized for her coverage of politics, race, and gender, as well as her calm presence; Rita Williams, a KTVU reporter, described her as having "so much class, so much presence, so much intuition" and called her "the grande dame." Her autobiography, Never in My Wildest Dreams: A Black Woman's Life in Journalism, was published in 2010, with Bill Cosby writing in the foreword that she had symbolic value to the African-American television audience, noting that "we looked forward to seeing her prove the stereotypical ugliness of those days to be wrong." Davis married Frank Davis on January 1, 1952, and had two children and a granddaughter. She met her second husband, Bill Moore, in 1967 while working at KPIX-TV, and they lived in Presidio Heights and later in Petaluma, California. Davis maintained a separation between her personal and professional life, allowing African-American woman and American Women in Radio and Television member Kathleen H. Arnold (now anthropologist Kathleen Rand Reed) to produce Belva Davis – This is Your Life in 1975, and mentored Reed for decades. She served on the boards of the Museum of the African Diaspora, the Institute on Aging, and the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, raising $5 million for the Museum of the African Diaspora in one year. Davis won eight Emmy Awards from the San Francisco/Northern California chapter and was an honorary member of Alpha Kappa Alpha. She received lifetime achievement awards from the American Women in Radio and Television and the National Association of Black Journalists. She died in Oakland, California, from a long illness on September 24, 2025, at the age of 92.
